items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the downslope movement of weathered material under the influence of gravity”.
items.answer: Mass movement
items.markingKey: Mass movement: the downslope movement of weathered material under the influence of gravity. [1]

items.stem: Explain how heavy rainfall can trigger a landslide.
items.answer: Water adds weight (shear stress); high pore-water pressure pushes particles apart, reducing friction and cohesion (shear strength); lubricates slip planes; erosion of the slope foot.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain the process of soil creep.
items.answer: Particles are lifted at right angles to the slope by wetting or freezing (heave) and fall back vertically under gravity when they dry or thaw, so they move slowly downslope.

items.stem: Engineers estimated the shear strength and shear stress (kPa) on three slopes along a mountain road in Nepal. Slope A: shear strength 59, shear stress 73. Slope B: shear strength 102, shear stress 68. Slope C: shear strength 108, shear stress 104. Explain how heavy rainfall could change the factor of safety.
items.answer: Water adds weight (increasing shear stress) and raises pore water pressure (reducing shear strength), so the factor of safety falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that water is the most important factor in causing mass movement. In your answer you may refer to human activity, earthquakes and pore water pressure.
items.answer: For: Rain and snowmelt raise pore water pressure and weight; most landslides follow heavy rain (e.g. Kerala 2018, Uttarakhand 2013); mudflows need saturation. Against: Slope angle, rock structure (bedding dipping out of the slope), weathering, earthquakes, undercutting by rivers or waves and human activity (road cuts, deforestation, loading) also matter; rockfalls can be dry. Conclusion: Water is the most common trigger, but slopes fail only where geology, angle and human activity have already reduced stability.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “mass movement”?
options: The movement of a mass of material along a curved slip plane, often on clay.
The rapid free fall of rock fragments from a steep cliff face.
The downslope movement of weathered material under the influence of gravity.
The very slow downslope movement of soil particles by heave, mainly caused by wetting and drying or freezing and thawing.
items.answer: The downslope movement of weathered material under the influence of gravity.
items.markingKey: Mass movement: the downslope movement of weathered material under the influence of gravity. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All mass movements are rapid events.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Soil creep is extremely slow, perhaps only millimetres a year.

items.stem: Classify mass movements by speed and water content.
items.answer: Heaves (creep) slow and moderately wet; flows (mudflows, earthflows) fast and wet; slides (rotational, translational) fast, moderately dry along a slip plane; falls very fast and dry.

items.stem: Explain why rotational slides are common on clay slopes.
items.answer: Clay becomes saturated and loses strength; it is weak and impermeable, so water builds up; slopes over-steepened by river or wave erosion fail along a curved plane.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Vegetation always makes slopes less stable.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why rotational slides are common on clay slopes.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Roots usually bind soil and transpiration dries it, increasing stability; very large trees can add weight and wind stress. (b) Clay becomes saturated and loses strength; it is weak and impermeable, so water builds up; slopes over-steepened by river or wave erosion fail along a curved plane.

items.stem: Explain how rainsplash causes the net movement of soil downslope.
items.answer: Raindrops detach particles and splash them in all directions; on a slope those moving downslope travel further and those moving upslope a shorter distance, so there is net downslope movement.

items.answer: Contour ploughing; terracing; mulching or cover crops; stone lines (bunds); agroforestry; strip cropping.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that rainsplash and sheetwash are more important than mass movement in shaping slopes.
items.answer: For: On gentle slopes in semi-arid and cultivated areas rainsplash and sheetwash remove topsoil continuously and shape pediments. Against: On steep slopes, mass movement (landslides, rockfall, creep) moves far more material; humid vegetated slopes have little wash. Conclusion: Their importance depends on climate, vegetation and slope angle: wash dominates on gentle, bare slopes, mass movement on steep ones.

items.stem: Explain how human activities can make slopes less stable.
items.answer: Undercutting by road and building construction steepens slopes; adding weight (buildings, tipping waste) increases shear stress; leaking pipes and irrigation raise pore water pressure; deforestation removes roots; vibrations from traffic or blasting.

items.stem: Explain how vegetation can stabilise slopes.
items.answer: Roots bind soil and increase shear strength; interception and transpiration reduce soil moisture and pore water pressure; protects surface from rainsplash.

items.answer: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: Alerta Rio warning system with sirens; Geo-Rio slope works, retaining walls and drainage; relocation of some households; reforestation; limited by cost and continued informal building.

items.stem: Aisha argues that human activities are now the main cause of slope instability. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to deforestation, earthquakes and rainfall.
items.answer: For: Road cuts, quarrying, construction, deforestation, irrigation and leaking water pipes trigger many landslides, e.g. in the Himalaya, Hong Kong and Rio de Janeiro. Against: Natural factors (heavy rain, earthquakes, weathering, undercutting by rivers and waves, slope angle and geology) remain the main causes in remote mountain areas. Conclusion: Human activity is increasingly important near settlements and roads, but natural triggers still cause most slope failures globally.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the process of soil creep. (b) Explain how heavy rainfall can trigger a landslide.
items.answer: (a) Particles are lifted at right angles to the slope by wetting or freezing (heave) and fall back vertically under gravity when they dry or thaw, so they move slowly downslope. (b) Water adds weight (shear stress); high pore-water pressure pushes particles apart, reducing friction and cohesion (shear strength); lubricates slip planes; erosion of the slope foot.

(b) Water adds weight (shear stress); high pore-water pressure pushes particles apart, reducing friction and cohesion (shear strength); lubricates slip planes; erosion of the slope foot.

items.stem: Nadia argues that water is the most important factor in causing mass movement. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Rain and snowmelt raise pore water pressure and weight; most landslides follow heavy rain (e.g. Kerala 2018, Uttarakhand 2013); mudflows need saturation. Against: Slope angle, rock structure (bedding dipping out of the slope), weathering, earthquakes, undercutting by rivers or waves and human activity (road cuts, deforestation, loading) also matter; rockfalls can be dry. Conclusion: Water is the most common trigger, but slopes fail only where geology, angle and human activity have already reduced stability.

items.stem: A surveyor measured an unstable cut slope above a road in Dubai’s hinterland. It rises 14.4 m over a horizontal distance of 25 m. (a) Explain why regrading increases slope stability. (b) Suggest why regrading may not be possible here and suggest an alternative.
items.answer: (a) A lower angle reduces the downslope component of gravity (shear stress), so the factor of safety increases. (b) Space is limited by the road and buildings, and land is costly; alternatives include soil nailing, rock bolts, retaining walls, drainage or vegetation.
